tool.name: ThiessenPolygonsConvex
tool.summary: Creates Thiessen (Voronoi) polygons from points: each polygon is the area closer to its point than to any other point. The polygons are exact vector cells clipped to a rectangle, a convex polygon or the points' extent expanded by a percentage. Each polygon carries the source ObjectID, the number of points at that location and its area in square metres. Works on a Basic licence, no extension.

param.name: clip_extent
param.dialogReference: Optional rectangle the polygons are clipped to. Four numbers (xmin ymin xmax ymax, separated by spaces, with a decimal point) are read in the input's coordinate system; an extent taken from a layer or the map carries its own system and is projected. ArcGIS Pro parses typed extent text itself before the tool gets it (Pro 3.3.2 read 499990,5 in an arcpy script call as 499990.5), so the tool cannot refuse a decimal comma there: type a decimal point. Only when the extent reaches the tool's code as text (the tool run outside Pro's geoprocessing, as with the simulated arcpy of the tests) does the tool read it itself: then commas between the four numbers are also accepted and a decimal comma is refused. Use Clip Features instead for a study area that is not a rectangle.

param.name: clip_features
param.dialogReference: Optional layer with one convex polygon (your study area) the polygons are clipped to (select one feature if the layer has several). Without a clip, the points' extent grown by Expand % is used.

param.name: expand_pct
param.dialogReference: Without a clip: grow the points' extent by this percentage on each side (0 to 1,000,000). Disabled and not checked when a clip is given.

param.name: copy_attributes
param.dialogReference: Copy the attributes of each point (the lowest ObjectID at a duplicated location) to its polygon.

param.name: out_features
param.dialogReference: Output polygon feature class: SITE_OID, DUP_COUNT, AREA_M2 plus the point attributes.

tool.usage:
In short: choose the point layer. With no clip, the polygons are cut at the points' extent grown by Expand % (default 10 %), which leaves large cells at the edge; to get your study area, give a Clip Extent, or one convex polygon in Clip Features (for example a rectangle or a convex hull). The output is written in the measuring system (see below: a projected input keeps its own system and units, for example US feet) with SITE_OID, DUP_COUNT and AREA_M2 (always square metres). Large inputs take a while: roughly one minute for 50,000 points in the Python core (not measured in Pro); the progress bar counts the kept point locations (duplicates and merged points are not built).

Clip: give a Clip Extent or one convex Clip Feature (a single polygon without holes, for example a rectangle or a convex hull), not both. Without either, the points' bounding box is grown on each side by Expand % of its width (left and right) and height (bottom and top); points on one straight line use the other dimension; points almost on one line give a box thinner than 1/1000 of its length, and a warning then says the polygons are slivers (give a clip). Expand is at most 1,000,000 %, and a clip (given or grown) larger than 100,000 km across is refused: the polygons would lose precision. Concave clip polygons are not supported in this version. Convexity is checked in the clip's own coordinate system: the clip counts as convex when no vertex lies deeper inside its convex hull than one millionth of its size (at least 0.5 mm, for coordinates rounded to the geodatabase resolution), and it is then replaced by that hull; a clip in another system than the measuring system is replaced by the convex hull of its projected vertices. A Clip Extent without a coordinate system (typed as four numbers) is taken in the input's coordinate system; an extent that carries a coordinate system (for example one taken from a layer or the map in the dialog) is projected from that system, and the rectangle around its projected corners in the measuring system is used (an edge that follows a parallel can bow outside it).

Points at the same location are merged: the lowest ObjectID keeps the polygon (SITE_OID) and DUP_COUNT counts all of them; the others are listed in a warning (at most 20 locations, largest first, and 20 merged OIDs per location). Points outside the clip still shape their neighbours' polygons; a point whose polygon lies completely outside the clip gets no polygon and is listed. The cells are exact up to rounding: a polygon edge lies within about one billionth of the clip size of the true bisector (0.1 mm in a 100 km clip). ArcGIS Pro stores the vertices on the output's XY resolution grid (0.1 mm by default) and cleans each polygon with the XY tolerance (1 mm by default): a polygon less than about 3.5 XY tolerances wide is stored empty. So the points are taken in ObjectID order and a point closer than ten times the XY tolerance (1 cm by default) to a kept point is merged into the nearest kept point like a duplicate (DUP_COUNT counts it, its attributes are not copied), with a warning; such a point can lie a few millimetres inside a neighbouring polygon. Every polygon is then at least 10 XY tolerances wide, except where the clip cuts it. The tolerance is the one of the output as created: the XY Tolerance environment or a feature dataset in the same coordinate system can set it (the output is then built again with it, with a message). An output in a feature dataset in another coordinate system than the measuring system is refused and deleted: its XY tolerance would be in other units (for example degrees) and ArcGIS Pro would project the polygons; write it outside the feature dataset. In an unknown coordinate system (for example a shapefile without a .prj) the unit is not known (it may be degrees), so the merge distance is only 3.5 XY tolerances (0.0035 data units by default) and the warning gives it in data units. The stored shapes are read back and a polygon that is not one ring is named in a warning (this can still happen for a point within a few millimetres of the clip edge, or outside it); such a polygon is still counted in Polygon Count.

Polygons are built in a projected system chosen from the data (the input system, in its own units such as US feet, when it is already projected, else the matching UTM zone in metres; for a geographic input on another datum than WGS 84, the UTM zone on its own datum when EPSG defines one (for example Ain el Abd 1970 / UTM zone 38N), else the WGS 84 UTM zone with a warning that no datum transformation is applied (older datums such as NAD27 or ED50 can then be offset by up to several hundred metres: project such data to a projected metric system first); Web Mercator family inputs (e.g. WKID 3857), which distort distances, are re-projected to the UTM zone too, and data near the poles to a polar stereographic system), and the output is written in that system and its units. AREA_M2 is always in square metres, whatever the units of that system. For geographic (or Web Mercator) data wider than 3 UTM zones, polar data (beyond 84N / 80S) and input in a polar stereographic system, whose scale is not 1 over the data, the polygons are still built in that one system, but AREA_M2 is measured polygon by polygon on its own projection (Transverse Mercator centred on it, or polar stereographic with true scale at it near the poles; WGS 84 ellipsoid). Data wider than 10 UTM zones, and points that cannot be projected to the system, stop the run with a fix (project the points to a system suited to their extent first). Between 4 and 10 UTM zones the polygon edges are the bisectors in that one system (a message says so).

Speed: many points spaced evenly on one circle (co-circular) are slow, because every such point is a neighbour of every other: in the Python core (CPU time, not an ArcGIS Pro run time) 2,000 such points took 2.5 s near the origin and about 5 to 9 s at UTM coordinates, and 8,000 took 59 s near the origin. Ordinary data can reach this: stations spaced evenly along a ring road or another circular layout are nearly co-circular (8,000 chainage stations on a long arc of a 20 km curve took about 110 s of CPU time, 2,000 took 0.9 s); run such data in parts (a selection) or thin it. Scattered point data (addresses, facilities, samples) is not affected. A clip with many vertices is slow too: the time grows with points x clip vertices (a review measured 500 points with 20,000 clip vertices: 10.8 s of CPU time); simplify a densified clip first.

Clip Features in an unknown coordinate system (for example a shapefile without a .prj) cannot be projected: the run stops when the input has to be projected; when the input is used in its own system they are taken to be in it, with a warning. A copied field keeps its field-level domain when the output geodatabase has it, as Copy Features does (a warning names the fields that lose it); subtypes and subtype-level domains are not carried. Fields of the types GlobalID, Blob, Raster, Time Only and Timestamp Offset, and fields that are not editable, are not copied (no message). A user field named like a geometry field, such as Shape_Leng or Shape_Area from a shapefile export, is copied like any other field, possibly under another name (a shapefile output stores a user field Shape_Area as Shape_Ar_1; a message names it). A copied text field wider than a shapefile allows (254 bytes as ArcGIS Pro writes them: an Arabic letter takes 2, a character above U+FFFF such as an emoji takes 6 bytes, not the 4 of UTF-8; Pro's default length is 255) is written as wide as its longest value in bytes, at most 254, to a folder output; a longer value stops the run before anything is written. In a shapefile, copied field names are cut to 10 characters (Population_2020 becomes Population) and a warning names every field stored under another name; the fixed fields SITE_OID, DUP_COUNT and AREA_M2 are never changed. The names are read back from the output before writing: if ArcGIS Pro stored a field under another name than predicted (for example an Arabic name cut by bytes), the values go to the stored field and a warning names it.

Not checked or not done: a Basic licence is the target but is NOT VERIFIED; AREA_M2 is the planar area in the measuring system (for example UTM), not the area on the ellipsoid, except for wide or polar data (the planar area is up to about 0.2 % larger than the ellipsoid area near the edge of a UTM zone, less near its centre); the clip must be convex; 64-bit ObjectIDs above 2,147,483,647 make SITE_OID a Big Integer field in a geodatabase (an ObjectID above 2^53 - 1 stops the run) and, in a shapefile, a Double field while every ObjectID has at most 12 significant digits, else a text field of 20 characters with every digit kept (not verified in Pro); the tool does not poll for Cancel, so cancelling during the build is not reliable (not verified in Pro).

Selections and definition queries on the input layers are honoured. The input is never edited. If an arcpy error stops the run while the output is written, the output this run created is deleted and the messages collected so far are shown before the error.

Built-in alternatives: Create Thiessen Polygons is Basic: No, Standard: No, Advanced: Yes; Generate Weighted Voronoi needs the Spatial Analyst extension and creates its polygons from a Voronoi raster.
